governanceNotes: D1 batch 51 (2026-09-24): one bounded association edge authored - laryngeal stenosis to sleep-apnea (rank 1) - classified ASSOCIATION_ONLY with etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, vaNexusProbabilityAlignment NOT_ASSERTED, and hypothesizedOnly:true; mechanismCategory MECHANICAL_OR_COMPRESSIVE. The proposition rests on the Lackey 2025 cross-sectional pilot cohort of twenty adults with non-traumatic subglottic stenosis (all female, mean age 48.4 years, mean body-mass index 24.1, 80% idiopathic), in which every subject completed peak expiratory flow measurement, the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, and one night of home sleep testing, and which found obstructive sleep apnea in 40% of subjects (15% moderate), poor sleep quality (PSQI at or above 5) in 70%, and excessive daytime sleepiness (ESS above 9) in 20%, concluding that obstructive sleep apnea prevalence is elevated in this cohort and that screening and surveillance may need to be considered; it rests also on the Gadkaree 2017 case series of 262 adults with laryngotracheal stenosis, in which obstructive sleep apnea appears among the prevalent comorbidities of the iatrogenic cohort alongside type II diabetes, hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and stroke history, and in which iatrogenic aetiology, Cotton-Myer grade 3-4 stenosis, and lack of intraoperative steroids were associated with tracheostomy dependence. Narrowed laryngeal airway calibre and obstructive sleep apnea are thus documented to co-occur in the same patient populations.

Counter-evidence and caveat screens recorded 2026-09-24: (i) direction is not established - the Gadkaree series lists obstructive sleep apnea among pre-existing comorbidities in iatrogenic stenosis rather than as an outcome, so the co-occurrence may reflect shared risk factors or reverse influence rather than stenosis causing apnoea; (ii) small pilot - the Lackey cohort is twenty subjects at a single tertiary centre without a matched control group, and the authors present it as a pilot requiring further study of whether airway dilation affects apnoea; (iii) no dose-response demonstrated - peak expiratory flow percentage did not correlate with the apnoea-hypopnea index in that cohort; (iv) symptom measures did not separate groups - PSQI and ESS did not differ between subjects with and without apnoea; (v) shared risk factors - body-mass index, other airway diagnoses (laryngomalacia, tracheomalacia, vocal-fold pathology, and adenotonsillar hypertrophy), sedative and opioid exposure, and gastro-oesophageal reflux independently cause or aggravate obstructive sleep apnoea in the same populations.

Negative screens recorded 2026-09-24: (i) no laryngeal-stenosis-to-systemic-lupus-erythematosus edge - the harvested proposition remains FINAL-CLOSED under FINAL-CLOSE-PROPOSITION-MISMATCH and the established direction runs from the autoimmune disease to laryngeal involvement (prior-closure and direction guards); (ii) no aphonia, vocal-cord-dysfunction, vocal-cord-paralysis, or spasmodic-dysphonia edge - no condition-specific quantification for those outcomes was retrieved and those identities carry their own windows (zero-record and duplicate-scope guards); (iii) no dysphagia edge - the located swallowing literature addresses procedures and reconstruction in mixed airway populations rather than stenosis-specific swallowing outcomes (zero-record guard); (iv) no tracheostomy-dependence, respiratory-failure, or airway-obstruction edge - no such catalog identity exists and tracheostomy is a treatment step rather than a disease identity (absent-identity guard); (v) no asthma or vocal-cord-dysfunction misdiagnosis edge - the mimicry literature concerns diagnostic error rather than a secondary diagnosis (wrong-target guard); (vi) scope note: the separately catalogued tracheal-stenosis identity authors its own windows, and this subglottic window sits on the laryngeal identity because the subglottis is a laryngeal structure.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The Lackey 2025 cross-sectional pilot cohort of twenty adults with non-traumatic subglottic stenosis (all female, mean age 48.4 years, mean body-mass index 24.1, 80% idiopathic) completed peak expiratory flow measurement and validated sleep questionnaires with one night of home sleep testing and found obstructive sleep apnea in 40% of subjects (15% moderate), poor sleep quality in 70%, and excessive daytime sleepiness in 20%, concluding that obstructive sleep apnea prevalence is elevated in subjects with subglottic stenosis and that screening and surveillance may need to be considered, while peak expiratory flow percentage did not correlate with the apnoea-hypopnea index; the Gadkaree 2017 case series of 262 adults with laryngotracheal stenosis documents obstructive sleep apnea among the prevalent comorbidities of the iatrogenic cohort alongside type II diabetes, hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and stroke history; the literature documents elevated obstructive sleep apnoea prevalence in patients with a narrowed laryngeal airway without establishing that the stenosis caused an individual's sleep apnoea.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level: the pilot cohort is twenty subjects at one tertiary centre without a matched control group and its authors call for further study of whether airway dilation affects apnoea, peak expiratory flow did not correlate with the apnoea-hypopnea index, symptom scores did not distinguish subjects with and without apnoea, the larger case series records apnoea as a prevalent pre-existing comorbidity rather than an outcome of stenosis, and body-mass index, coexisting airway diagnoses, sedative or opioid exposure, and gastro-oesophageal reflux independently cause obstructive sleep apnoea in the same populations - so no directional claim is made.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized fixed-narrowing route is described: reduced laryngeal and subglottic cross-sectional area raises upper-airway resistance and increases the negative inspiratory pressure needed to move air, which promotes pharyngeal and supraglottic collapse during sleep and can produce obstructive events; the located pilot cohort found obstructive sleep apnoea in 40% of subjects with non-traumatic subglottic stenosis with poor sleep quality in 70%, a prevalence the authors judged elevated, but because the apnoea may equally precede or coexist with the stenosis and shared risk factors are unadjusted, the individual causal direction remains a hypothesis.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: This relationship is supported as an association only. Obstructive sleep apnoea prevalence is documented as elevated in a twenty-subject subglottic-stenosis cohort and apnoea is recorded among prevalent comorbidities in a 262-patient laryngotracheal-stenosis series, but individual determination requires airway documentation with grading, polysomnography, assessment of shared risk factors, and consideration of competing causes, with review by a qualified medical professional.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Airway documentation establishing the stenosis with date of onset or diagnosis, aetiology (iatrogenic after intubation or tracheostomy, autoimmune, idiopathic, traumatic, or neoplastic), anatomic level and length, and grading (for example Cotton-Myer grade) with endoscopic and imaging findings and any prior airway surgery or dilation; polysomnography or home sleep testing with the apnoea-hypopnea index, oxygen desaturation, and the study date, together with the time relationship between the stenosis diagnosis and the sleep study; documentation of daytime symptoms and validated questionnaire scores with dates; assessment of shared and competing risk factors including body-mass index and weight trajectory, nasal obstruction, adenotonsillar hypertrophy, craniofacial anatomy, sedative, opioid, or alcohol exposure, thyroid disease, and gastro-oesophageal reflux; identification of other airway lesions (laryngomalacia, tracheomalacia, vocal-fold pathology, or tracheal stenosis) that could independently produce obstruction; sleep-medicine, pulmonology, or otolaryngology assessment of whether the documented stenosis materially contributed to the obstructive sleep apnoea
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Obesity and weight gain as independent drivers of obstructive sleep apnoea
Another airway lesion (adenotonsillar hypertrophy, laryngomalacia, tracheomalacia, vocal-fold pathology, or nasal obstruction)
Sedative, opioid, or alcohol exposure and central sleep apnoea syndromes
Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with airway irritation
Hypothyroidism or acromegaly as endocrine contributors
Positional or REM-predominant obstructive sleep apnoea

evidenceGaps: Airway documentation establishing the stenosis with date of onset or diagnosis, aetiology (iatrogenic after intubation or tracheostomy, autoimmune, idiopathic, traumatic, or neoplastic), anatomic level and length, and grading (for example Cotton-Myer grade) with endoscopic and imaging findings and any prior airway surgery or dilation; polysomnography or home sleep testing with the apnoea-hypopnea index, oxygen desaturation, and the study date, together with the time relationship between the stenosis diagnosis and the sleep study; documentation of daytime symptoms and validated questionnaire scores with dates; assessment of shared and competing risk factors including body-mass index and weight trajectory, nasal obstruction, adenotonsillar hypertrophy, craniofacial anatomy, sedative, opioid, or alcohol exposure, thyroid disease, and gastro-oesophageal reflux; identification of other airway lesions (laryngomalacia, tracheomalacia, vocal-fold pathology, or tracheal stenosis) that could independently produce obstruction; sleep-medicine, pulmonology, or otolaryngology assessment of whether the documented stenosis materially contributed to the obstructive sleep apnoea
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY: a twenty-subject pilot cohort with home sleep testing found obstructive sleep apnoea in 40% of patients with non-traumatic subglottic stenosis with elevated screening scores, and a 262-patient laryngotracheal-stenosis series records apnoea among prevalent comorbidities, but the pilot is small and uncontrolled, its flow measure did not correlate with apnoea severity, the larger series describes apnoea as pre-existing, and shared risk factors are unadjusted; the conservative standard therefore keeps the edge at association only and avoids the FINAL-CLOSED lupus proposition and the direction-inverted autoimmune framing.
